summary: AI-Scientist makes every LLM request from nine lines in ai_scientist/llm.py, plus aider's coding calls through LiteLLM. Six of those nine now go to Router and three stay on their vendor for reasons Router cannot change (no llama model in the catalog; Gemini ids need the caller's own Google credential). Getting there needed four things beyond wrapping the clients: a model map, because the pipeline's default --model (claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620) and its hardcoded reviewer (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) are not catalog ids, so without it the migration would have moved no traffic at all; dropping seed=0, which made every GPT request untranslatable to Responses; porting the 5-way review ensemble off n=5, which has no Responses equivalent and kept the two most expensive calls per idea on OpenAI; and a compatibility fix, because the unpinned anthropic dependency has since dropped temperature from messages.create(), so the default Claude path raised TypeError before any request left the process. aider's traffic -- by far the largest share of tokens -- is routed through the LiteLLM hook, which reaches its OpenAI-provider calls only. Every routed path was checked against the real Router: /v1/messages on claude-sonnet-4-6 and /v1/responses on gpt-4o both 200, with the model map, the drop and the spend labels applied, and a repeated review-shaped prefix caching 11,904 of 12,036 tokens for 49% less per call.
reviewed: The review walked the pipeline stage by stage against what Router offers and asked where the model choice, the prompt shape or the control flow is wrong rather than merely unrouted. It looked at the token profile of each stage (ideation 50 ideas x 3 rounds, novelty up to 10 rounds per idea each re-sending the whole of experiment.py, 20 citation rounds, 11 review calls per paper run twice, and aider over a growing LaTeX file), at which Router levers each surface can actually reach, at the two calls that were being spent on stale or unusable context, and at the failure modes that discard an idea after its experiments have already run. Four improvements are built and measured against the real Router; eight are proposed, held back because each needs a judgement a human should make -- a different model's effect on idea, review or code quality, or a change to how the pipeline is structured.

items.title: Route the shared LLM clients in ai_scientist/llm.py
items.summary: create_client() builds one client per vendor for the whole pipeline; wrap_anthropic / wrap_openai put that traffic on Router, with the DeepSeek host unlocked.
items.gains: One Router key and one spend view for every stage of the pipeline, per-request provider fallback, and the Responses levers on the GPT paths. The app is unchanged until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set, and ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it off again.
items.loses: nothing
items.price: no change by itself; the model maps m3-m5 are what change the price
items.why: Every LLM request in this product is made from one of nine lines in llm.py, all using clients from create_client(), so wrapping that one function covers ideation, the novelty check, citation selection and paper review in a single edit. The Bedrock and Vertex clients are left alone, as the runtime refuses them by design.

evidence.detail: real Router: /v1/messages 200 model=claude-sonnet-4-6 provider=anthropic (the default path), /v1/responses 200 model=gpt-4o provider=openai (the reviewer)
router-migrate check --all: 7 of the 9 scanner-visible sites route; the two that do not are the OpenRouter/llama branches
compileall + import of all six modules: 10 passed, same as the baseline

items.title: Drop seed=0 on Router-bound OpenAI requests
items.summary: router.policy.json drops seed from the Router-bound copy of every GPT request, because seed makes a Chat Completions request untranslatable to Responses.
items.gains: The three GPT branches reach Router at all. Without it every GPT call in the pipeline -- paper review, the pinned gpt-4o reviewer, the o-series option -- stayed on OpenAI.
items.loses: OpenAI's best-effort sampling determinism on that path. These calls run at temperature 0.75 (0.1 for the reviewer, 1 for the o-series), so repeat runs already differed; seed is advisory even at temperature 0. The provider-fallback copy is unchanged and still carries seed.
items.why: Router has no Chat Completions endpoint and its Responses API returns 400 for seed, so the runtime classes those requests untranslatable and hands them to OpenAI unchanged. Dropping the parameter in policy rather than in the code keeps the fallback path byte-identical to what the application built.

evidence.detail: before: 'stays: untranslatable: seed' on lines 96/202/218; after: the same three sites ROUTE
real Router: /v1/responses 200 on the reviewer path with the policy applied

items.title: Serve the default Claude model with claude-sonnet-4-6
items.summary: Maps claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 and -20241022, which are not catalog ids, to claude-sonnet-4-6.
items.gains: The pipeline's default path routes. --model defaults to claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 for ideation, the novelty check, citation selection and aider, so without this map the migration moves essentially no traffic.
items.loses: A newer model writes different ideas, search queries and reviews than Claude 3.5 Sonnet did; prompts tuned against the old model may need revisiting.
items.price: claude-sonnet-4-6 is $3/$15 per 1M, the same as the model it replaces; cache reads $0.30 per 1M
items.why: Router serves undated catalog ids only, and neither Claude 3.5 Sonnet date is one (confirmed: 'not in the Router catalog'). claude-sonnet-4-6 is the same price and, unlike the cheaper claude-sonnet-5 at $2/$10, still accepts temperature -- the pipeline relies on 0.75 for idea diversity and 0.1 for the reviewer, and Router returns 400 for temperature on models whose catalog marks it unsupported.

evidence.detail: live catalog: claude-sonnet-4-6 $3/$15 temperature=true; claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10 temperature=false; claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 absent
real Router: create_client('claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620') produced /v1/messages 200 model=claude-sonnet-4-6 provider=anthropic

items.title: Serve the pinned reviewer gpt-4o-2024-05-13 with gpt-4o
items.summary: Maps the reviewer's hardcoded dated id, and the one review_iclr_bench offers, to the catalog's gpt-4o.
items.gains: Paper review -- 11 calls per paper, run again after the improvement pass -- reaches Router.
items.loses: A later snapshot of gpt-4o scores papers slightly differently, so review scores are not comparable with runs from the pinned May 2024 snapshot. That matters here: the score feeds the idea archive that generate_next_idea reads.
items.why: launch_scientist.py hardcodes model="gpt-4o-2024-05-13" for both review passes, and that id is neither a catalog id nor in Router's dated-id table, so the reviewer would stay on OpenAI. gpt-4o is the catalog id of that family, still active, and still accepts temperature, which the reviewer needs for ensemble diversity (0.75) and for the meta-review and reflections (0.1).

evidence.detail: live catalog: gpt-4o $2.50/$10 temperature=true status=active; gpt-4o-2024-05-13 absent and not in dated_equivalents
real Router: the reviewer's calls arrived as model=gpt-4o

items.title: Serve the DeepSeek options with their catalog successors
items.summary: Maps deepseek-chat and deepseek-coder to deepseek-v4.1-flash and deepseek-reasoner to deepseek-v4-pro-0813.
items.gains: The DeepSeek --model options route, so the host unlock added with m1 does something.
items.loses: A different model generation answers those runs -- a larger jump than the Claude and GPT maps, since the v3-era chat/coder/reasoner split no longer exists. Reverting this entry alone sends the DeepSeek options back to DeepSeek with the rest of the migration intact.
items.why: None of the three ids is a catalog id, so with the host unlocked but no map those requests would still go straight to DeepSeek. review_iclr_bench's own deepseek-coder-v2-0724 option is deliberately left unmapped and stays on DeepSeek.

evidence.detail: create_client('deepseek-reasoner') produced one valid /v1/responses request, model=deepseek-v4-pro-0813
live catalog: both targets temperature=true; deepseek-chat/coder/reasoner absent

items.title: Route the review clients in the launch scripts and ICLR bench
items.summary: Wraps the openai.OpenAI() clients built inline for paper review in launch_scientist.py, experimental/launch_oe_scientist.py and review_iclr_bench/iclr_analysis.py.
items.gains: Review traffic from every entry point routes, not just traffic from clients create_client() built.
items.loses: nothing
items.why: launch_scientist.py builds a fresh openai.OpenAI() inline for each paper review and each post-improvement re-review, and review_iclr_bench builds its own per-worker client instead of reusing create_client(). None of them went through create_client(), so wrapping llm.py alone left them on OpenAI. The OpenRouter and Gemini clients in the same functions are deliberately left on their vendors (see s1, s2).

evidence.detail: compileall + import of all six modules: 10 passed
the review-shaped path these clients serve was exercised live: /v1/responses 200 model=gpt-4o

items.title: Route aider's coding traffic through the LiteLLM hook
items.summary: install_litellm() in the three entry points hands LiteLLM a routed session, so aider's experiment and writeup calls go to Router when the model is an OpenAI-family id.
items.gains: The pipeline's largest share of tokens becomes visible and routable: up to 4 iterations x 5 experiment runs, about 45 writeup passes over a growing LaTeX file, plus the improvement pass, each carrying the whole file context.
items.loses: nothing
items.why: aider talks to models through LiteLLM, which builds its own HTTP clients, so no SDK wrap reaches it. The hook is the runtime's sanctioned entry point for that. It is a no-op until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set.

evidence.detail: a real Coder.run() with Model('gpt-4o-mini') produced one valid /v1/responses request on the simulator and returned the model's answer

the hook does not reach LiteLLM's Anthropic provider: with Model('claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620') 0 requests reached the simulator and api.anthropic.com was contacted twice. Patching litellm.module_level_client did not change that. On the default --model, aider's traffic still goes to Anthropic; item i6 is the way to move it.

items.title: Port the 5-way review ensemble from n=5 to one call each
items.summary: The GPT branch of get_batch_responses_from_llm handles n_responses == 1 only; an ensemble falls through to the per-response loop that Claude and the other vendors already used.
items.gains: The two most expensive calls per idea reach Router. perform_review runs with num_reviews_ensemble=5 for every paper and again for every improved paper, and the ensemble path is the same for every vendor now.
items.loses: Input tokens are charged per reviewer instead of once. The review prompt is about 20k tokens (review form, one few-shot paper, the paper), so on gpt-4o the step goes from roughly $0.13 to $0.23 per ensemble before caching. The shared prefix is identical across all five, so m9's cache key puts the four repeats on cache reads; it also costs five round trips instead of one, which improvement i4 removes.
items.price: about +$0.10 per ensemble review on gpt-4o before caching, roughly halved by m9
items.why: Router's Responses API has no n, so the runtime classed those requests untranslatable (measured: 'untranslatable: n', 3 provider requests, 0 to Router) and the single largest prompt in the pipeline never reached Router. Dropping n in policy instead would have silently returned 1 review where the code expects 5 and degraded the ensemble without saying so.

evidence.detail: before: 'provider (runtime kept it) ... untranslatable: n' x3. After: 5 valid /v1/responses requests, model=gpt-4o, and get_batch_responses_from_llm still returned 5 responses
20k-token prompt on gpt-4o at $2.50/$10: n=5 was $0.050 input + $0.075 output; five calls are $0.150 input uncached, $0.075 with m9's cache reads at $1.25/1M

items.title: Prompt cache key and product spend tag on routed requests
items.summary: router.policy.json sets prompt_cache_key "$feature" and metadata.product on every Router-bound Responses request.
items.gains: Half the input cost on every repeated prefix, and the pipeline is attributed as one product in Router's usage views.
items.loses: nothing
items.price: measured 49% less per repeated review-shaped call on gpt-4o
items.why: Every stage re-sends a large constant prefix -- the novelty check repeats a system message holding the whole of experiment.py for up to 10 rounds per idea, the ideation loop repeats the task description and the same code, each review repeats the review form plus a few-shot paper -- and Router does not cache on the Responses path without a key.

evidence.detail: real Router, gpt-4o, three identical 12,036-token calls: call 1 cached 0 tokens at $0.03011; calls 2 and 3 cached 11,904 tokens at $0.01523 each

items.title: Port the Claude call to the installed Anthropic SDK
items.summary: temperature moves into extra_body on client.messages.create(), because current anthropic versions no longer accept it as a named argument.
items.gains: The pipeline's default path runs at all, and can therefore be routed and verified.
items.loses: temperature is no longer type-checked by the SDK, so a model that does not support it fails at the API instead of at the call site. The model map in m3 deliberately targets claude-sonnet-4-6, which the catalog marks as accepting temperature.
items.why: requirements.txt pins no anthropic version and current releases (1.13.0 in this environment) dropped temperature from Messages.create()'s signature while the API still honours it as a body field. Every Claude call raised TypeError before any request left the process -- pre-existing, not caused by this migration, and it made the default --model path impossible to route or verify. extra_body is accepted by both the pre-1.0 and current SDKs.

evidence.detail: before: TypeError: Messages.create() got an unexpected keyword argument 'temperature'. After: real Router /v1/messages 200, model=claude-sonnet-4-6, provider=anthropic, and a two-turn conversation returned both answers
10 passed, same as the baseline

items.title: The OpenRouter llama option stays on OpenRouter
items.summary: Router lists no llama model, so meta-llama/llama-3.1-405b-instruct requests keep going to openrouter.ai.
items.gains: nothing changes for this option
items.loses: nothing
items.why: The runtime routes a request only when its model is a Router catalog id. There is no llama entry in the live catalog, so the client is left unwrapped rather than carrying a host unlock that could never fire. A human who wants this traffic on Router has to pick a different model for it.

evidence.detail: openrouter.ai was contacted 3 times and nothing reached Router
live catalog: no llama id; nearest open-weight options are gpt-oss-120b $0.15/$0.60 and nemotron-3-ultra $0.60/$2.40

items.title: The Gemini options stay on Google
items.summary: Router's Gemini ids all require the caller's own Google credential, so they are not servable by a Router key alone.
items.gains: nothing changes for this option
items.loses: nothing
items.why: Every gemini id in the live catalog is marked requires_byok, which the runtime excludes from its catalog entirely, so no Gemini request can resolve to Router. Note the scanner reports this line as routing; it does not -- the client is unwrapped and generativelanguage.googleapis.com is not an unlocked host.

evidence.detail: generativelanguage.googleapis.com was contacted 3 times and nothing reached Router
live catalog: all 12 gemini ids requires_byok=true

items.title: The Bedrock and Vertex Claude clients stay on their clouds
items.summary: AnthropicBedrock and AnthropicVertex clients are left untouched, as the runtime refuses them by design.
items.gains: nothing changes for these options
items.loses: nothing
items.why: wrap_anthropic returns Bedrock and Vertex clients unchanged. Router does list Bedrock Claude ids, but they are requires_byok and would need the caller's own AWS credential, which is what those clients already use directly.

evidence.detail: runtime contract: 'Azure, Bedrock and Vertex clients' stay on the provider, unchanged

items.title: Label every call with the pipeline stage it belongs to
items.summary: get_response_from_llm and get_batch_responses_from_llm take an optional feature= and send it as the x-router-migrate-feature header; callers pass ideation, novelty, citations, review, review-reflection and review-meta.
items.gains: Spend is attributed per stage instead of per helper function, per-stage settings in router.policy.json become possible at all, and the policy's prompt_cache_key "$feature" starts resolving per stage so the novelty check's experiment.py prefix no longer shares a cache key with the reviewer's few-shot paper. This is the mechanism i3, i4 and i7 need.
items.loses: Six more call-site arguments to keep in step as stages are added or renamed; a stale label silently falls back to the policy defaults rather than erroring.
items.why: Every stage funnels through the same two helpers, so Router saw the whole product under two stack-derived labels (ai_scientist/llm.py:get_response_from_llm and :get_batch_responses_from_llm). A pipeline whose stages differ by 30x in difficulty and by orders of magnitude in volume cannot be reasoned about, priced or tuned through one label. feature defaults to None, so untouched callers behave exactly as before, and providers ignore an unknown header when the pipeline is not on Router.

evidence.detail: real Router, 4 calls, 4 labels, both surfaces: /v1/messages feature=novelty and feature=ideation on claude-sonnet-4-6, /v1/responses feature=review and feature=review-meta on gpt-4o
10 passed, same as the baseline

items.title: Cache the large repeated prefixes on the Claude path
items.summary: The system prompt becomes a cacheable block when it is over about 1,024 tokens, and each prompt gets a breakpoint at its end so the next turn reads the earlier turns from cache.
items.gains: Measured against the real Router: a 10-round novelty check drops from about $0.43 to $0.09 in input cost, roughly 78% less, and a 3-round ideation reflection loop about 52% less. With 50 ideas per run and up to 10 novelty rounds each, this is the largest cost line in the pipeline after aider.
items.loses: The first call in each conversation pays 1.25x input for the cache write, so a prefix used exactly once costs 25% more. Both loops here re-use theirs at least twice, and a template whose experiment.py is under ~1,024 tokens gets no benefit and no penalty.
items.why: The Claude path goes over Router's /v1/messages, where Router's own prompt_cache_key does not apply -- so the pipeline's two biggest repeated prefixes were charged at full input price on every call. Block-level cache_control works on both the pre-1.0 and current Anthropic SDKs and is the form Router passes through; the caller's own message history is left unmarked so breakpoints cannot accumulate past Anthropic's limit.
items.price: claude-sonnet-4-6 cache reads are $0.30 per 1M against $3 input

evidence.detail: real Router, claude-sonnet-4-6, 57.7k-character novelty system message: round 1 wrote 14,438 tokens to cache; rounds 2 and 3 read 14,429 and sent 3 uncached input tokens
short-system case (ideation): two turns both 200, and no cache markers leaked into the returned history
10 passed, same as the baseline

items.title: Stop spending calls on stale context and dying on recoverable gaps
items.summary: Fixes three places where the pipeline paid for a call it could not use or discarded an idea that had already cost hours: the no-papers novelty round, repeated novelty queries, and two crashes in the review aggregation.
items.gains: When Semantic Scholar returns nothing, the novelty check no longer spends the remaining rounds re-reasoning over the previous query's papers -- up to 9 of 10 full-context rounds per idea. An ensemble where nothing parsed fails immediately with the reason instead of spending a meta-review request on an empty list and then raising IndexError; a score field no reviewer filled in no longer raises 'cannot convert float NaN to integer'. Either crash surfaced as 'Failed to perform review' and threw away a finished experiment and writeup.
items.loses: A review whose ensemble produced no usable number for a field now carries the meta-reviewer's own value for it rather than failing, so a caller that assumed every numeric field was an ensemble average no longer always gets one.
items.why: check_idea_novelty fell into enumerate(None) when a search returned nothing, and its exception handler left papers_str holding the previous round's results. perform_review's aggregation assumed at least one parseable review and at least one in-range numeric score per field. None of this involves Router; it is the cheapest value in the ranking because it removes calls and failures outright.
items.price: removes LLM calls; no price change per call

evidence.detail: 10 passed, same as the baseline

with a stub client and no provider: an all-unparseable ensemble raises ValueError naming the count after exactly 3 requests (no meta-review call); string scores aggregate; out-of-range and missing scores are ignored; int(round(np.mean([]))) confirmed to raise on the old path

items.title: Issue the review ensemble's requests together
items.summary: The per-response loop uses a bounded thread pool, so a 5-reviewer paper review is one round trip's wait instead of five.
items.gains: Measured 3.60s to 0.75s for a 5-response ensemble through Router, 4.8x faster, and it recovers the latency m8 cost to get that step routed. It applies to Claude and every other vendor, which already used this loop.
items.loses: Up to 5 concurrent requests per ensemble. review_iclr_bench already runs batch_size worker processes that can each hold an ensemble open, so its ceiling becomes batch_size x 5 requests, and Router records usage after the fact, so concurrent requests can overshoot a spend cap. AI_SCIENTIST_ENSEMBLE_WORKERS=1 restores the sequential behaviour.
items.why: The ensemble members are independent samples of the same prompt on the largest prompt in the pipeline; there is no reason to wait between them. Order is preserved so msg_histories[0] is still the first reviewer, and n_responses == 1 takes the direct path unchanged.

evidence.detail: real Router, gpt-4o, 10 live calls: 3.60s with max_workers=1 against 0.75s with max_workers=5, 5 histories returned in order
10 passed, same as the baseline

items.title: Serve Claude over Responses so the Router levers apply
items.summary: When Router is active, build the Claude path on a wrapped OpenAI client so the request is translated to /v1/responses instead of going to /v1/messages.
items.gains: Unlocks, for the pipeline's default path, every lever that is Responses-only today: a models fallback list, provider_timeout, metadata spend tags, usage.cost on each response, and Router's own prompt_cache_key. At present roughly all of the pipeline's non-aider traffic runs on the Messages surface, where only the model id, model_map/drop_params and the feature header apply -- so most of what Router offers is simply unavailable to this product.
items.loses: Two code paths in create_client, because an OpenAI client cannot serve a Claude model without Router: the Anthropic SDK must remain the path when RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is unset, so the default path's behaviour would differ between the routed and unrouted runs. The Chat-to-Responses translation also changes some request details (tools become strict-explicit, client-side stop emulation), and i2's cache_control markers would need replacing with Router's cache key.
items.why: This is the single biggest structural limit the migration found. The product's default model is Claude, Claude through the Anthropic SDK lands on /v1/messages, and that surface carries none of Router's request-level controls. Everything else proposed here -- fallbacks for a multi-hour run, a bounded provider timeout, per-call cost reporting -- is blocked behind this one choice. It is a rework because it changes which SDK serves the default path and needs a deliberate decision about behaving differently with and without Router.
items.price: no direct change; enables the fallback and timeout work

evidence.detail: every live Claude call in this migration logged 'router-migrate policy not applied on /v1/messages (Router-only fields are Responses-only; model_map applies)'
no side-by-side of answer quality or request shape between the two surfaces for this pipeline's prompts

items.title: Give aider a catalog model so its traffic routes
items.summary: Pick a Router catalog coding model for aider instead of passing the pipeline's --model id through to LiteLLM.
items.gains: Moves the largest share of the product's tokens onto Router. aider drives the experiment loop and about 45 writeup passes over a growing LaTeX file; on the default --model none of it routes today, so the majority of spend stays outside Router's key, spend views and fallbacks. It would also let the coding model be chosen on its merits -- gpt-5.3-codex at $1.75/$14 or deepseek-v4-pro-0813 at $1.32/$3.96 against claude-sonnet-4-6 at $3/$15.
items.loses: A different coding model changes aider's edit quality and how reliably it produces applicable SEARCH/REPLACE blocks in the diff edit format the pipeline depends on; a model aider does not know well can fail to edit at all, which fails the experiment loop. It also splits the --model flag's meaning: one model for reasoning stages, another for coding.
items.why: install_litellm() reaches LiteLLM's OpenAI-provider calls only. Measured: Model('gpt-4o-mini') routes end to end, while Model('claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620') produced 0 Router requests and went to api.anthropic.com -- LiteLLM's Anthropic handler builds clients the hook cannot reach, and patching litellm.module_level_client did not change that. Choosing an OpenAI-family catalog model for aider is the clean way in; reaching into LiteLLM's internals is not.
items.price: depends on the model chosen; gpt-5.3-codex $1.75/$14, deepseek-v4-pro-0813 $1.32/$3.96, gpt-4.1-mini $0.40/$1.60

evidence.detail: a real Coder.run() with Model('gpt-4o-mini') produced one valid /v1/responses request through the hook
Model('claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620') and Model('anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6'): 0 requests to Router, api.anthropic.com contacted twice
no comparison of edit success rate or experiment-loop completion between coding models

items.title: Pick the model per stage instead of one model for everything
items.summary: Use a cheap model for the stages that emit short structured JSON (novelty queries, citation selection, idea reflections) and keep the strong model for ideation quality, coding and review.
items.gains: The largest cost reduction available without changing what the product does. The novelty check's job per round is to emit one search query and a novel/not-novel verdict, and citation selection is picking indices from a list -- both currently run on a $3/$15 model. claude-haiku-5-5 is $0.10/$0.50 and gpt-4o-mini $0.15/$0.60, 20-30x cheaper, and these are the two highest-call-count stages in the pipeline (up to 500 novelty rounds and 40 citation calls per run). router.policy.json can do it per stage with model_map, no code change.
items.loses: A weaker model writes worse search queries, so the novelty verdict gets less reliable -- and a wrong 'novel' verdict sends an idea into hours of GPU experiments. Citation selection errors show up as wrong or missing citations in the paper. Which stages can take the cheaper model is a quality judgement that should be measured on this pipeline's own prompts, not assumed.
items.why: One --model for all six stages prices the easiest work at the hardest work's rate. With i1's labels in place this is a few lines of policy, and each stage can be moved independently and reverted independently.

evidence.detail: live catalog prices per 1M: claude-haiku-5-5 $0.10/$0.50, gpt-4o-mini $0.15/$0.60, gpt-5.4-nano $0.20/$1.25, claude-sonnet-4-6 $3/$15
no measurement of novelty-verdict agreement or citation-selection accuracy between a haiku-class and a sonnet-class model on this pipeline's prompts

items.title: Fall over to a second vendor on the reviewer
items.summary: Add a models fallback list for the review stage in router.policy.json, so a provider outage does not end a run at its last step.
items.gains: A paper still gets reviewed when one vendor is down. Review is the final step after experiments and writeup, so a failure there is the most expensive failure in the product: do_idea catches the exception and returns False, discarding hours of GPU time and every token already spent on that idea.
items.loses: Scores from a different vendor are not comparable with the rest of the run, and the score is written into the idea archive that generate_next_idea reads, so a fallback review would quietly skew the open-ended loop. Router does not report which candidate served, so a run cannot tell afterwards that it happened -- that is the main reason this is proposed rather than built.
items.why: The review stage is on the Responses surface, so the fallback lever is available today without i5. The capability guard keeps candidates that cannot take temperature out of the list, which leaves gpt-4.1 at $2/$8 and claude-sonnet-4-6 as workable second choices.
items.price: the serving candidate's price, only when it serves

evidence.detail: live catalog: gpt-4.1 $2/$8 temperature=true; claude-sonnet-4-6 $3/$15 temperature=true; both pass the policy's capability guard for a temperature-bearing request
fallback behaviour on a real provider outage is documented by Router but not measured here

items.title: Raise the output cap for the review stage
items.summary: MAX_NUM_TOKENS is 4096 for every call; the review stage needs more headroom than the rest.
items.gains: A review that hits the cap is truncated mid-JSON, extract_json_between_markers returns None, and the reflection's assert fails -- so the whole 20k-token call is paid for and thrown away, and with i3's guard an all-truncated ensemble now fails the paper outright. The review schema asks for a THOUGHT section plus 16 fields including a summary, a strengths list, a weaknesses list, questions and limitations, which is the only prompt in the pipeline plausibly near 4096 output tokens.
items.loses: Output tokens are the expensive half ($10 per 1M on gpt-4o, $15 on claude-sonnet-4-6), so a higher cap lets a verbose review cost more; you pay for what is generated, not for the cap.
items.why: One constant caps every stage, and the stages' output shapes are nothing alike -- a novelty round emits a one-line query, a review emits a structured document. Raising it only for review keeps the others as they are.
items.price: no change to the rate; more output tokens possible on the review stage

evidence.detail: reasoned from the review schema's size, not measured: no instrumented count of how often a real review hits 4096 output tokens. Worth measuring before applying -- the finish_reason or an incomplete status would show it

items.title: Drop the unused google.generativeai import
items.summary: ai_scientist/llm.py imports genai and GenerationConfig and never uses either; Gemini is served through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
items.gains: Removes a dependency from the import path of every entry point and the FutureWarning it prints on every run ('All support for the google.generativeai package has ended'). The package is deprecated upstream, so it is a scheduled break in a required dependency for no functionality.
items.loses: Nothing in the code. Anyone who relied on importing ai_scientist.llm to pull google.generativeai in as a side effect would no longer get it, and requirements.txt would want the line removed too.
items.why: Confirmed unused: the only occurrences of genai or GenerationConfig in the repository are the two import lines. The gemini branches of create_client and get_response_from_llm go through openai.OpenAI with Google's OpenAI-compatible base URL and never touch the SDK.

evidence.detail: repository-wide search: genai and GenerationConfig appear only at ai_scientist/llm.py:8 and :9; the deprecation FutureWarning appears in every test and probe run in this session

items.title: Checkpoint each phase so a late failure keeps the work
items.summary: do_idea runs experiments, writeup, review and improvement in one try block and returns False on any exception, discarding everything.
items.gains: The experiments are the expensive part -- up to 5 GPU runs with a 2-hour timeout each, plus every aider call that produced them. Today a writeup error, a review that will not parse or a LaTeX failure throws all of it away and the idea cannot be resumed; re-running means paying for the experiments again. Phase-level checkpoints would let a run resume at the failed phase.
items.loses: State to manage: a partially finished idea folder is now a thing the code has to recognise, validate and resume from, and a resumed run can mix outputs from two different model versions or two different Router routings. The parallel worker path and the results-directory layout both need to understand it.
items.why: This is the product's largest single waste and it is not an LLM problem -- but it determines what every LLM failure costs, which is why it belongs in this ranking. It is a rework because it changes the pipeline's control flow and on-disk contract, not a call or a parameter.
items.price: no change per call; avoids re-paying for completed phases

evidence.detail: read from launch_scientist.py do_idea: each phase's except returns False with no record of what completed; perform_experiments already writes run_i folders and notes.txt, so the data needed to resume largely exists

items.title: Bound provider calls and retry the failures that matter
items.summary: Nothing bounds how long a single call may take, and the backoff decorator retries only RateLimitError and APITimeoutError.
items.gains: A hung provider call cannot stall a multi-hour run indefinitely, and a 429 or 5xx on one call stops ending a phase. Router's provider_timeout sets the bound server-side, per candidate.
items.loses: A Router timeout comes back as a plain-text 504 with no JSON body, which the current backoff does not catch -- so adding provider_timeout without widening the retry would convert slow calls into hard failures and make things worse. The two halves have to land together, and a retry on a non-idempotent phase can double-charge a call that actually succeeded upstream.
items.why: provider_timeout is a Responses-only field, so on the default Claude path it needs i5 first; on the GPT paths it is available today. Pairing it with a widened retry is what makes it safe, which is why this is a change rather than a quick-win.
items.price: no change; truncated attempts are still billed

evidence.detail: read from llm.py: backoff.on_exception lists only openai.RateLimitError and openai.APITimeoutError, and no timeout= is set on any client or call; Router's maximum provider_timeout is 660s
no measurement of how this pipeline's calls behave against a provider_timeout, or of the 504 shape under the current backoff

items.title: The meta-reviewer's numeric scores are all discarded
items.summary: perform_review overwrites all nine numeric fields of the meta-review with the ensemble's own averages, so that call contributes text only.
items.why: After get_meta_review returns, the loop over Originality, Quality, Clarity, Significance, Soundness, Presentation, Contribution, Overall and Confidence replaces each one with int(round(mean(ensemble))). The meta-reviewer is therefore paid a full-paper request to produce a Summary, Strengths, Weaknesses, Questions, Limitations and Decision; its scores are computed by the code regardless. Worth knowing before anyone tries to improve review calibration by prompting the meta-reviewer differently, and worth deciding deliberately -- either the averages are the intent and the prompt should stop asking for scores, or the meta-reviewer's judgement should be allowed to override them.

evidence.detail: read from ai_scientist/perform_review.py: the score loop assigns review[score] unconditionally after get_meta_review
